sources.citation: Imtiaz, Mashrur. 2026. 'Language, power, and the erasure of Kol.' The Daily Star (Dhaka), Slow Reads special (Amar Ekushey issue), 21 February 2026.
sources.note: No phonology content. Sociolinguistic/decolonial essay: naming (Kol vs 'Santali' umbrella), Munda substrate words in Bangla (Chatterji), borrowing from Santali and Bangla, GIDS level 6-7, language shift among the young, Roman script 'with special diacritic markers' now used to write Kol, call for documentation and community teaching.

sources.citation: Rashid, Mohammad Mamun Or. 2026. Oral to Web: Digitizing 'Zero Resource' Languages of Bangladesh. arXiv:2603.05272 [cs.CL] (v2, 6 March 2026). EBLICT Project, Bangladesh Computer Council / Jahangirnagar University. (Describes the Multilingual Cloud Corpus: 85,792 IPA-transcribed entries + ~107 h audio, 42 varieties incl. Kol.)
sources.note: Nothing on prosody (my search of the full HTML text: stress 0, tone 0). Kol content is corpus statistics: 2,443 textual entries (Bengali stimulus, English translation, IPA transcription) with aligned audio, 514 isolated words, sentence topics 19-21/21; notes that Kol has an 'established writing system' yet is classed endangered by IMLI (2018). Value: points to the first open primary audio + IPA data set for Bangladesh Kol (multiling.cloud), from which stress could be measured, and cites IMLI 2018 'Ethno-linguistic survey of endangered languages of Bangladesh' (the print survey already on our…

sources.citation: Bangladesh Computer Council (ICT Division), EBLICT / Languages of Bangladesh (LOB) project. 2025-. 'Kol / কোল' - language profile and digital archive (directed-sentence recordings with IPA transcription, Bengali and English glosses; 5 speakers, 800 sentences, c. 250 minutes). In: Multiling Cloud: Digital Archive of Ethnic Languages of Bangladesh (web archive, launched July 2025).
sources.note: No phonological description at all: a one-paragraph sociolinguistic blurb (classification, speaker number, shift to Bengali, scripts, oral literature) plus the archive counters. The archive itself (800 IPA-transcribed, audio-aligned directed sentences; dictionary-word and spontaneous-speech sections empty for Kol as of 2026-09-21) is primary data, not a statement; whether the IPA marks stress could not be checked because items load by JavaScript (no ˈ or ˌ in the served HTML).

sources.note: Short uncited phonology paragraph: 5 vowels as in Mundari, each with short/long/nasal allophones, length and nasalization not contrastive; 'broad pronunciation'; open monosyllables longer than closed ones; 23 consonants (stops, nasals, fricatives, approximants, tap); consonant clusters only word-initially; and one prosodic remark: NO TONE ('not being Mon-Khmer, tone does not exist here') but 'definite intonation patterns', 'in this respect Kol follows Mundari'. Nothing whatsoever on word stress/accent (no শ্বাসাঘাত/ঝোঁক/stress term on the page). Recorded as has_statement=false because it neit…

sources.citation: মুহাম্মদ হাবিবুর রহমান (Muhammad Habibur Rahman). 2014. বাংলাদেশের নানান ভাষা [The many languages of Bangladesh]. ঢাকা: প্রথমা প্রকাশন (Prothoma Prokashon). ISBN 978-984-90660-9-5. Section 'কোল', pp. 81-83 (chapter 'অন্যান্য ক্ষুদ্র জনগোষ্ঠীর ভাষা').
sources.note: No phonology content. The Kol section (Bengali, popular register; originally serialized in Prothom Alo, Feb 2013) says: the Kol live in a few small villages of Rajshahi, Chapainawabganj, Naogaon, Joypurhat and Dinajpur; 'কোলদের নিজস্ব ভাষা থাকলেও বর্ণমালা নেই। বাংলা ভাষার প্রভাবে কোল ভাষার সঙ্গে অনেক বাংলা শব্দের সংমিশ্রণ ঘটেছে' (they have their own language but no script; many Bengali words have mixed); lists words shared by Santali and Kol (ফুল 'baha', ভাত 'daka', পানি 'dao', বলদ 'dangra', মহিষ 'kara', ছাগল 'merom', ভেড়া 'bhedi'), kin terms ('aiyo' parents), greeting 'ডোবো', and a 'thubra'…
